## Environmental Variables
This section goes over what environmental variables we are using for our iSSFs. In this example, we will be using a two class (dense and sparse/bare) map of submerged aquatic vegetation (SAV) mapped using aerial imagery flown over our study site. The map was made using photointerpreted points to train a Random Forest algorithm on the spectral information within the aerial imagery. We will be using this map to also calculate spatial pattern metrics using the dense class of SAV, which are measures of composition and configuration of the seascape. Included in this section will also be the setup of the data for iSSFs, including calculating the "false" steps that the iSSFs use to determine habitat selection.

We will end up with 6 environmental variables: class of SAV, PLAND (Percentage of Landscape that the dense SAV class makes up), Edge Density (the density of edges of the dense SAV class), Patch Density (the density of patches of the dense SAV class), Division (a measure of likelihood that two randomly selected cells are not the same patch), and Mean Shape (a measure of how complex the patches of dense SAV are). This is where you can substitute any environmental data you may have based on your questions. 

```{r}
#Load in libraries
library(amt) #Package that iSSFs are in
library(tidyverse)
library(survival)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(furrr) #for parallel processing for landscape metrics. Makes it much quicker
library(purrr)
library(ggeffects)
library(landscapemetrics) #package for calculating spatial pattern metrics

rdat <- read_csv('data/interpolated_hmm_states_30min.csv')
rmap <- rast('maps/rmap_dense.tif')

plot(rmap)

# Make fish tracks with the amt functionality
fish_trackr <- rdat %>%
  mutate(ID = as.factor(ID),
         ts = as.POSIXct(ts, format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%OS", tz = "UTC")) %>% 
  make_track(
    .x = x, # X coordinate column
    .y = y, # Y coordinate column
    .t = ts, # Timestamp column
    id = ID, # Individual ID column
    crs = st_crs(rmap),
    state = state)

# Convert the track to observed steps, grouped by track
# This calculates step length (sl_) and turn angle (ta_) for the observed steps. You have to nest by ID or else 
#it thinks it is one long track
steps_obsr <- fish_trackr %>%
  # Isolate each fish's track into a list-column called 'data'
  nest(data = -id) %>%
  # Apply steps() to each nested track independently
  mutate(
    step_data = map(data, ~ steps(.x, keep_cols = "start"))
  ) %>%
  # Keep only the ID and the new step data, then expand back to a normal dataframe
  select(id, step_data) %>%
  unnest(cols = step_data)
```

## Generating random steps for iSSFs

Now that we have our observed data set up for environmental extraction and iSSF calculation, we need to calculate the random steps that the iSSFs need to compare against our observed step. In this workshop, we are just going to do a 10 - 1 ratio, but in the actual paper we are using a 100 to 1 ratio. This will lead to lower error in the model, but take A LOT longer.

```{r}
# Generate random steps (10 random steps for every 1 observed step)
steps_randr <- steps_obsr %>%
  random_steps(n_control = 10)

#We have our random steps, now we need to extract the habitat variables at the end of each step - The HMM state is preserved across each step
head(steps_randr)

sr <- steps_randr %>% drop_na() %>% dplyr::mutate(ID = 1:n()) #drop NAs and create an ID column to calculate spatial pattern metrics across
```

## Extracting environmental data

We have our data in the format we need to both extract classes and run spatial pattern metrics on them. However, do you remember when we told you that the environmental data needs to match the resolution of your environmental data? Well, here is where it comes into play. For the extraction of SAV classes, we are going to use a kernel to calculate the class most present within a 10m x 10m square around each cell in our map. This mimics the 10m error we filtered by for our positions. We will then extract the class at each position using this new map.

```{r}
#create a kernel for the map to calculate the majority class with
kernel <- matrix(1, nrow = 31, ncol = 31)

#Apply the kernel across all of the cells in the original map and plot it
rmap_kernel <- focal(rmap, w = kernel, fun = "modal", na.rm = TRUE)

plot(rmap_kernel) #it reduces the complexity, but is better for fitting the data. We will use the complexity of the original map to calculate spatial pattern metrics

#create a spatialpointsdataframe and extract from map
sr2 <- st_as_sf(sr, coords = c("x2_", "y2_"), crs = st_crs(rmap_kernel)) %>% terra::extract(x = rmap_kernel, y = ., ID = F) %>% bind_cols(sr) %>% 
  mutate(class = if_else(focal_modal == 1,2,1)) %>% drop_na() %>% dplyr::select(-focal_modal)
```

If the class is 2, it is dense SAV and if it is 1, it is sparse SAV/bare sediment. Now that we have our classes extracted, we are going to calculate some spatial pattern metrics. To do this, we are going to calculate the 5 variables brought up in the intro: PLAND, ED, PD, Divisionm and Shape_mn.
